links.note: Asks which of two traits at 10% and 60% frequency arose earlier in an asexual population - the answer turns on variations building up over successive generations, so the older trait is the commoner one. That is accumulation of variation (206), not the creation of variation in a single reproductive event (205).
How creation of variations promotes survival: the item tests why reproduction throwing up subtle differences matters, which is 205. Not 206, which is about the build-up of frequency over generations.
Tall/violet x short/white, progeny all violet but half short, deduce TtWW. Two traits tracked at once, so it is the dihybrid cross (215); a monohybrid cross (212) would follow only one trait.

Equal genetic contribution of both parents is ensured because each gamete carries a single set of chromosomes and fusion restores the diploid number - that is exactly 219. Not 218, which is about genes sitting on chromosomes.

The 50:50 boy/girl ratio is explained by the father producing X- and Y-bearing sperm in equal numbers, i.e. the paternal contribution decides sex (221). 220 is the plainer XX/XY fact, which this item assumes rather than tests.
A woman with only daughters: the explanation is that only the father's X-bearing sperm happened to fertilise, so it is the paternal chromosome (221) rather than the XX/XY statement (220).
Progeny of the given crosses include a 9:3:3:1 round/wrinkled x yellow/green outcome - two traits, so dihybrid (215). Stem defect: the crosses themselves are missing from the stem text.
Lists the four F2 combinations and their 9:3:3:1 ratio - the dihybrid F2 result itself (215). The sibling item 86471, which asks WHY new combinations appear, is the independent-assortment one.
Asks the reason new character combinations appear in F2; the answer is independent assortment of the two gene pairs (216), which is the law, not the cross (215).
Why no two individuals in a population are alike - answer is reshuffling of genes during reproduction plus mutation, i.e. variation arising during reproduction (205).
F1 = first filial generation. The F1/F2 notation is introduced by and only meaningful within Mendel's monohybrid cross (212); 209 is about Mendel's method and standing, not the notation.

Part (b), the scored part, asks why variations are essential to a species - the value of the differences thrown up by reproduction (205). Part (a) is only the DNA acronym, which no concept here covers.
How organisms create an exact copy of themselves: reliable transmission of traits to offspring, which is the definition of heredity (207). Not 219, which is the chromosome-number mechanism.
PP x pp purple/white, F1 colour, 25% white in F2, PP:Pp 1:2 - one trait followed through F1 and F2, so monohybrid cross (212) rather than dominance alone (210).

Part (a): a surgically detailed mouse has normal progeny because the change is not in the genes of the germ cells - the answer turns on germ cells as the channel of inheritance (219). Part (b) is homologous/analogous organs, for which this chapter has no concept.
The blanks are gametes and genotypes of a T/t x R/r cross (Tr, tR, TtRr, tall round) - a two-trait cross, so dihybrid (215). Stem defect: the table the blanks belong to is not in the stem.
Boy or girl is a matter of chance because the father makes X- and Y-bearing sperm in equal proportion - the paternal chromosome (221), not the XX/XY statement (220).

Beetles stay small through poor nourishment but the third generation is normal: it tests which traits are inherited and which are merely acquired, so 208. Not 205, since no new variation is created here.
RR x rr round/wrinkled, F1 and F2 phenotypic 3:1 and genotypic 1:2:1 - a single-trait cross through two generations, so monohybrid (212).

Cousin marriage is dangerous because recessive defect alleles become homozygous and then express - that is precisely the recessive-trait rule of needing two identical copies (211), not dominance (210).

If both F1 characters passed together there would be no recombination and F2 would be 3:1 - the item tests independent assortment by asking what its absence would look like (216), not the dihybrid cross procedure (215).

Resemblance to parents exceeds resemblance to grandparents because each parent contributes one whole chromosome set through a germ cell (219). 218 would be the location of genes on chromosomes, which is not what is asked.

Parts (a) and (b) define homozygous and heterozygous, i.e. whether the two copies of Mendel's factor in an individual are identical or contrasting (213). Part (c) is speciation, for which this chapter has no concept.
Tails removed surgically, progeny all have tails: an acquired change is not an inherited trait (208). Sibling 205 is about variation arising in reproduction, which is not what the item turns on.

Asks what counts as a characteristic (photosynthesis, two eyes, multicellularity) - the definition of a trait/characteristic, which is 208. 207 is the transmission process, not the definition of the thing transmitted.
